questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly identifies the three traits that typically distinguish master data from other data an organization stores?
options: It's reused across multiple systems and processes, it changes slowly, and it's relatively low in volume but high in value
It's generated continuously by business activity, it's extremely high in volume, and it's defined by an external standards body
It's created once and never referenced again, it changes constantly, and it's low in value
It's reused across systems, it changes constantly like a transaction log, and it's always defined by an external standards body
It's low in volume, changes slowly, but is reused only within a single department, never across systems
It's high in volume, changes slowly, and is reused across systems and processes
questions.explain: Lesson 1 gives three traits that separate master data from the rest of what a company stores: it's reused, not generated once; it changes slowly; and it's relatively low in volume but high in value, since getting one customer record wrong can taint millions of order records built on top of it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F keeps 'changes slowly' and 'reused across systems' correct, but swaps the volume characteristic. Lesson 1 describes master data as relatively low in volume compared to the transactional data built on top of it (50,000 customers versus 50 million orders) — high volume is the hallmark of transactional data, not master data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 2, a specific instance of reference data — such as the complete list of valid country codes — is called a ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 2's key terms define a code list as a specific instance of reference data, giving the list of valid country codes as the example.

questions.prompt: Match each MDM architecture style from Lesson 3 to how it actually handles the data.
right: A central master store exists and syncs bidirectionally with source systems — changes flow in both directions
Source systems keep their own data as-is; a thin central layer stores only matching keys and cross-reference links
One central system becomes the actual system of record; source systems read from it instead of keeping separate copies
Master data is pulled into a central store and used for reporting, but the central store is never written back to source systems
questions.explain: Registry style keeps source data in place with only a thin cross-reference layer. Consolidation pulls data centrally but doesn't write back. Coexistence syncs bidirectionally. Centralized makes one hub the actual system of record for all writes.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 4, select every statement that correctly describes how to build a credible MDM business case.
options: A credible business case ties cost categories to something the organization can actually observe, like a known duplicate-mailing incident
A strong business case cites an independently-unverified industry statistic to make the pitch more persuasive
Mergers and acquisitions are a common driver that gets MDM programs funded, since combining two companies means combining data that was never designed to be compared
Regulatory and compliance pressure can be a legitimate driver for funding an MDM program
The strongest business cases are built from a borrowed statistic rather than the company's own citable pain
questions.explain: Lesson 4 explicitly says a credible business case ties cost categories to real, observable pain the organization has — a known incident, a reporting discrepancy, a current M&A integration — and names M&A and regulatory pressure as real drivers. It also explicitly warns against citing an unverified industry statistic, which rules out options B and E: the lesson states the strongest business cases are built from the company's own citable pain, not a borrowed number.

questions.prompt: A retailer's CRM, billing, and shipping systems each have a slightly different record for the same customer: different name spelling, different address, same phone number. Per Lesson 1, what does this scenario actually demonstrate?
options: Each system is individually correct about something, but none alone reliably answers 'who is this customer, right now' — exactly the gap MDM exists to close
One of the three systems must contain corrupted data, since a real customer can only have one true record
This is a reference data problem, not a master data problem, because it involves a status discrepancy
This situation only matters once the company starts using the data for a data warehouse load
questions.explain: Lesson 1's three-system customer example makes exactly this point: all three systems are technically correct about something, but none on its own is a reliable answer to 'who is this customer, right now' — that gap, not a single corrupted record, is what MDM exists to close.

questions.prompt: Lesson 3 describes the four MDM architecture styles as a spectrum of increasing central control (and increasing disruption to source systems). Put them in order from lowest control/disruption to highest.
items: Registry style
Consolidation style
Coexistence style
Centralized (transaction hub) style
questions.explain: Lesson 3 frames this explicitly as a spectrum from 'barely touch anything' (registry, the lightest touch) through consolidation (one-way central store) and coexistence (bidirectional sync) up to 'one system owns everything' (the centralized transaction hub, highest control and highest disruption).

questions.prompt: A company's million-row customer table would require roughly 500 billion pairwise comparisons to match every record against every other record. Per Lesson 6, what technique avoids this, and how?
options: Blocking — grouping records into smaller blocks by a coarse, cheap attribute like zip code first, then only running detailed matching within each block
Deduplication — deleting every record with a duplicate name before any matching runs
Survivorship rules — deciding in advance which source system's values always win, so matching never has to run
Golden records — building one combined record per customer before any comparison takes place
questions.explain: Lesson 6 introduces blocking specifically to solve this: grouping records into smaller blocks by a coarse, cheap-to-compute attribute first, then running detailed matching only within each block, which drops the comparison count from everyone-vs-everyone to a small fraction of that.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 6, the specific field or fields actually compared to decide whether two records represent the same entity — a tax ID, or a name-plus-address combination — is called a ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 6's key terms define a match key as the specific field or fields used to compare records, giving tax ID and name-plus-address as the common examples.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about deterministic versus probabilistic matching, per Lesson 7.
options: Deterministic matching is fast, simple, and fully explainable, but brittle once it relies on free-text fields like names
Probabilistic matching scores similarity across multiple fields and weights those scores into one overall confidence level
A probabilistic matching process typically uses a single cutoff score, not two thresholds
Most real MDM implementations use deterministic rules for the easy, certain cases and probabilistic scoring for everything else
String-similarity techniques like Levenshtein distance or Jaro-Winkler are used to compute how close two strings are, not just whether they're equal
questions.explain: Lesson 7 describes deterministic matching as simple, fast, and explainable but brittle on free-text fields, and probabilistic matching as weighted multi-field scoring that uses Levenshtein- or Jaro-Winkler-style similarity. It explicitly uses two thresholds, not one — so option C is false — and states most real implementations combine both approaches rather than picking just one.

questions.prompt: Match each survivorship strategy from Lesson 10 to the situation it actually describes.
right: A specific source is designated authoritative for an attribute regardless of recency, like the ERP for legal billing address
The value from whichever source last updated the field is used, sensible for a phone number or email
When the same value appears in more than one source, that agreement itself is used as evidence it's correct
When one source has a populated value and another is blank, the non-null value wins by default
questions.explain: 'Most recent wins' uses whichever source last updated the field. 'Trusted source wins' designates one source as authoritative regardless of recency. 'Most complete wins' prefers a populated value over a blank one. 'Most frequent wins' treats agreement across sources as evidence of correctness.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the overall match-to-golden-record pipeline from Chapter 2 in the correct order.
items: Group records into blocks by a coarse attribute so detailed matching doesn't compare every record to every other record
Apply deterministic rules first, wherever a trustworthy unique identifier exists
Score the remaining uncertain pairs probabilistically, weighting similarity across multiple fields
Route each pair's score to auto-match, no-match, or steward review based on the two thresholds
Assemble the golden record from the confirmed matches, deciding attribute by attribute which source's value survives
questions.explain: Chapter 2 builds this pipeline in exactly this order: blocking makes matching tractable at scale (Lesson 6), deterministic rules catch the easy cases first (Lesson 7), probabilistic scoring handles everything else, threshold routing decides auto-match/no-match/review (Lesson 7), and only then does survivorship assemble the golden record from the confirmed matches (Lessons 9-10).

questions.prompt: A probabilistic matching process scores a candidate pair of records and compares that score against two thresholds rather than one. What determines what happens to that pair?
options: Above the upper threshold it auto-matches, below the lower threshold it's called no match, and anything between the two is routed to a human steward for review
Above the upper threshold it's auto-rejected, below the lower threshold it auto-merges, and anything between the two is deleted
Only scores exactly equal to one of the two thresholds are ever acted on; everything else is ignored
The lower threshold determines auto-merge and the upper threshold determines no-match, with nothing in between
Both thresholds exist only to flag pairs for deletion; matching decisions are made separately
The two thresholds apply only to deterministic matching, never to probabilistic scores
questions.explain: Lesson 7 is explicit about this: above the upper threshold is confident enough to auto-match, below the lower threshold is confident enough to call no match, and the band in between is too uncertain to decide automatically, so it's routed to a human steward — and that middle band is deliberate, not a flaw.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B keeps the right shape — two thresholds, three outcomes — but swaps which threshold does what and invents an outcome ('deleted') the lesson never describes. The upper threshold is specifically the auto-match boundary and the lower threshold is specifically the no-match boundary, not the reverse, and neither threshold leads to deletion of a record.

questions.prompt: A match review system merges two records that turn out to be different real-world people, contaminating one customer's profile with a stranger's purchase history. Per Lesson 11, what is this outcome called, and how does it compare to the alternative failure mode?
options: A false positive — generally harder to detect after the fact than a false negative, which just leaves a quiet, unmerged duplicate behind
A false negative — the louder, more immediately obvious failure of the two
A true positive — the intended, correct outcome of the match process
A blocking failure — caused by grouping records into the wrong block before matching ever started
questions.explain: Lesson 11 defines a false positive as merging two records that are actually different entities — contaminating a customer's data and eroding trust once discovered, and hard to detect after the fact. A false negative, by contrast, is the quieter failure of leaving a true duplicate unmerged, which defeats MDM's purpose for that record but doesn't actively corrupt anything.

questions.prompt: A sole proprietor is both a paying customer and a supplier of the same company. Per Lesson 12's party model, how would an MDM system most naturally represent this?
options: As a single generic 'party' entity that holds two roles — customer and vendor — layered on top of it
As two entirely separate and unrelated database structures, one for individuals and one for organizations
As a customer record only, since a party model doesn't allow a person to also be a vendor
As a reference data entry, since roles like 'customer' and 'vendor' are classification codes
questions.explain: Lesson 12 describes the party model as a generic 'party' entity, person or organization, with roles like customer, vendor, or employee layered on top — and notes explicitly that the same party can hold multiple roles at once, giving a sole proprietor who is both a customer and a vendor as the example.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 13, a specific sellable variant of a product — one color, one pack size, one unit of measure, each with its own barcode and inventory count — is called a ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 13 defines a SKU (stock-keeping unit) as exactly this — a specific sellable variant of the broader, conceptual 'product,' tracked separately in inventory with its own barcode.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about vendor master data as a fraud-prevention control, per Lesson 14.
options: Duplicate vendor fraud involves creating a second record for a real vendor with different banking details, to redirect a payment
Sanctions screening against government watch lists is typically performed before a vendor master record goes live, not as a separate disconnected activity
Vendor onboarding should act as a gate on the master record, rather than letting any employee create a vendor ad hoc when they need a purchase order
Every vendor, regardless of spend or criticality, should receive the exact same level of review and a dedicated relationship owner
Banking and payment-terms data are the main reason vendor master sits closer to financial controls than most other master domains
questions.explain: Lesson 14 defines duplicate vendor fraud exactly this way, describes sanctions screening as a governance control layered onto vendor-master creation (not disconnected from it), argues onboarding should gate the master record, and names banking/payment-terms data as the reason vendor master sits closer to financial controls. Option D contradicts the lesson's vendor segmentation guidance, which explicitly says not every vendor warrants the same scrutiny — a strategic vendor gets a dedicated owner, a one-time office-supplies vendor gets a lighter-weight record.

questions.prompt: Match each master data domain to the detail Lessons 12-15 use to characterize it.
right: Attributes include remittance address, banking details, and payment terms, since money flows out to this party
Overwhelmingly sourced from one internal system (an HRIS), so matching and dedup is less of a burden than for other domains
Modeled with a party entity that can be a person or an organization, with roles layered on top
Distinguishes the conceptual item from its specific sellable variant, tracked at the SKU level
questions.explain: Customer master is built on the party model (person or organization with roles). Product master distinguishes the conceptual product from its SKU-level variants. Vendor master centers on banking and remittance data because money flows out to the vendor. Employee master is sourced overwhelmingly from the HR system, which is why it needs less matching and dedup effort than the other domains.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 13, put these levels of the product classification hierarchy in order from broadest to most specific.
items: Brand
Category
Subcategory
Product
SKU
questions.explain: Lesson 13's worked example runs brand ('Nike') down to category ('Footwear'), subcategory ('Running Shoes'), the specific product (a shoe model), and finally its size/color SKUs — broadest to most specific.

questions.prompt: A location master record has a stale address that no longer matches where a store actually operates. Per Lesson 15, what is one concrete consequence this lesson calls out?
options: A tax calculation engine could apply the wrong jurisdiction's tax rate, since some tax engines rely on an accurate location down to the geocode
The HR system would be unable to onboard any new employees anywhere in the company
The product classification hierarchy would need to be completely rebuilt from scratch
Reference data governance would automatically correct the address without any steward involvement
questions.explain: Lesson 15 states directly that a location record with a stale or wrong address 'doesn't just misdirect mail — it can misroute a shipment or miscalculate a tax liability,' specifically because tax calculation engines often need an accurate location, sometimes down to the geocode, to apply the correct jurisdiction's rate.

questions.prompt: A company tracks 'the list of valid order-status values' (a dozen possible codes) separately from 'the list of actual orders placed this week' (thousands of rows). Per Lesson 17's practical test, how should these two be classified?
options: The status-value list is reference data; the actual orders are transactional data
Both are reference data, since both involve a status concept
Both are master data, since both describe something the business tracks
The status-value list is transactional data; the actual orders are reference data
questions.explain: Lesson 17's practical test asks whether a record describes a thing, an allowed value, or an event. A short, stable, finite list of valid order-status values is reference data; the actual time-stamped orders are events, which is transactional data.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 18, a code that is no longer valid for new records, but is kept in the table so historical records can still resolve it, is called ________ rather than deleted.
questions.explain: Lesson 18's central point, illustrated with the PEND-to-RVW example, is that deprecating a code (marking it inactive for new use while keeping the row for old records to reference) is almost always preferable to deleting it outright.

questions.prompt: Select every element Lesson 19 says a reference data change request should document before approval.
options: The specific code being added, deprecated, or modified
Which systems consume this code list and need to be notified
The effective date the change takes hold
A directive that the old value be permanently deleted from the table the moment the new one is approved
What happens to historical data already using the old value
questions.explain: Lesson 19 lists exactly these elements for a usable change request: the specific code change, the business reason, which consuming systems need notification, the effective date, and what happens to historical data already using the old value. Option D contradicts Lesson 18's explicit deprecate-don't-delete guidance that Lesson 19 reinforces — a change request should describe deprecation, not deletion.

questions.prompt: Match each cross-reference mapping concept from Lesson 20 to its description.
right: A code with no corresponding row in the cross-reference table — should fail loudly, not pass silently
Each code in one system maps to exactly one equivalent code in another system
A code in one system could validly correspond to more than one code in another, depending on context
Multiple distinct codes in one system collapse into a single, less granular code in another — a lossy mapping
questions.explain: One-to-one mapping pairs each code with exactly one equivalent. Many-to-one collapses several distinct codes into one less granular code, which is lossy. Many-to-many means a code can validly map to more than one target depending on context. An unmapped value is a code with no row in the table at all, and Lesson 20 says that should fail loudly rather than pass through silently.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 21, put these steps of distributing a golden record via publish-subscribe in the correct order.
items: A golden record changes in the system of record after matching and survivorship rules resolve it
The system of record publishes the update to a central channel without needing to know who is listening
Consuming systems that subscribe to the relevant updates receive and apply the change on their own schedule
The distribution is monitored to confirm each consumer actually applied the update, not just that it was sent
questions.explain: Lesson 21 describes publish-subscribe distribution in this order: a golden record changes, the system of record publishes to a central channel without tracking subscribers, each subscribing consumer applies the update independently, and mature programs monitor distribution itself to confirm the update was actually applied downstream, not just successfully sent.

questions.prompt: System A adds a brand-new status code, but nobody updates the cross-reference table that maps System A's codes to System B's. Per Lesson 20, what is the better way for the integration to handle this unmapped value?
options: Make it a loud, visible failure — an error or an alert to the reference data steward — so the mapping gets added deliberately
Silently pass the unmapped code through unchanged, so the integration never has to stop
Silently default it to whatever value appeared most recently, so no one ever has to look at it
Permanently remove System A's new code so the mismatch can't occur again
questions.explain: Lesson 20 warns that silently passing through or defaulting an unmapped value hides the gap until a downstream report quietly produces wrong numbers. The better pattern is to make it a loud, visible failure that alerts the reference data steward, so the missing mapping gets added deliberately.

questions.prompt: Match each data quality dimension from Lesson 22 to its definition, as applied to a master data record.
right: Whether a populated value conforms to its defined format or domain, like a two-letter state code
Whether required fields are actually populated, like a missing email address
Whether the same fact agrees across fields or systems, like a vendor shown active in one system and terminated in another
Whether a value reflects reality, like a ship-to address that's complete but out of date
questions.explain: Completeness asks whether required fields are populated. Accuracy asks whether a value reflects reality, even if it's populated. Consistency asks whether the same fact agrees across systems. Validity asks whether a populated value conforms to its defined format or domain.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 23, the integration mechanism where a hub publishes a change ('Customer 48291 updated') onto a message bus and interested systems react on their own schedule is called ________ integration.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 names this mechanism event-driven / publish-subscribe integration — it decouples the hub from needing to know who its consumers are, since the hub simply publishes and subscribers react independently.

questions.prompt: A team is comparing MDM tools and leaning toward Microsoft SQL Server Master Data Services (MDS) mainly because it's familiar. Per Lesson 24, what should give them pause?
options: Microsoft has removed MDS starting with SQL Server 2025, continuing to support it only in SQL Server 2022 and earlier
MDS has never supported hierarchies, unlike Reltio or Informatica
MDS can only be used for reference data, never for master data
MDS requires an organization to already be using SAP ERP
questions.explain: Lesson 24 explicitly flags that Microsoft has removed MDS starting with SQL Server 2025, continuing to support it only in SQL Server 2022 and earlier — a concrete, current reason not to default to a tool purely because it's familiar, since tool landscapes shift even when the underlying MDM concepts don't.

questions.prompt: The Brightfield Outdoor Supply case study in Lesson 25 walks through this course's five chapters in order. Put these case-study milestones in the order they actually happened.
items: Leadership discovers three different systems give three different answers for 'how many wholesale customers do we have'
The team matches and deduplicates customer records across the website, CRM, and POS, collapsing about 40,000 records to roughly 31,000 real customers
Customer, product, and vendor master domains are tackled one at a time, uncovering issues like a vendor set up as two separate records
A single managed code list replaces three inconsistent country/state code lists across the old systems
The team settles on a coexistence architecture with event-driven distribution and a quality scorecard owned by the VP of Operations
questions.explain: The case study follows the course's own chapter order: Chapter 1 exposes the problem through a disagreeing headcount, Chapter 2 matches and deduplicates the underlying records, Chapter 3 tackles customer/product/vendor master one domain at a time, Chapter 4 standardizes the drifted reference code lists, and Chapter 5 settles the architecture, distribution mechanism, and quality ownership.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about fixing master data problems, per Lessons 22 and 23.
options: Pushing validation back to the point of capture is the durable fix; cleansing rules inside the hub are a safety net, not a strategy
A record can be perfectly deduplicated — exactly one golden record per entity — and still be low quality if that record has missing or stale fields
A nightly batch feed that was fine at low volumes can start failing in practice once usage patterns demand fresher data
Picking an integration mechanism is a one-time technical decision that never needs revisiting once it's made
Matching and deduplication alone guarantee high data quality, so a quality scorecard is redundant once Chapter 2's work is done
questions.explain: Lesson 22 argues for fixing validation at the source rather than patching it in the hub, and distinguishes matching/dedup ('how many records') from quality ('is this one record any good') — a perfectly deduplicated record can still be incomplete or stale. Lesson 23 explicitly says picking an integration mechanism is a bet worth revisiting whenever usage patterns change, directly contradicting option D, and nothing in either lesson supports option E's claim that a scorecard becomes redundant once dedup is done.
